passages.t: Zeal without knowledge, and ‘Christ is the end of the law’
passages.happening:
Paul begins again with his heart. “Brothers, my heart’s desire and prayer to God for the Israelites is for their salvation” (verse 1).

He speaks well of them. “For I testify about them that they are zealous for God, but not on the basis of knowledge” (verse 2). They did not know the righteousness that comes from God, and they tried to set up their own. So they did not submit to God's righteousness (verse 3).

Then comes one of the most debated lines in the letter. “For Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Paul prays for his people. That alone tells the Gentile believers in Rome how to think of the Jews who had not believed: as people to pray for, not people to scorn.

‘Zealous for God’ is praise, not mockery. Zeal means burning devotion. Paul knew it well, because he had had it himself. He tells the Philippians that before he met Christ he was “as to zeal, persecuting the church” (Philippians 3:6). In Acts he says, “I am just as zealous for God as any of you here today” (Acts 22:3). When Paul says ‘zeal without knowledge’, he is describing his own former life as much as anyone's. He was sincere, devoted, and wrong about Jesus.

‘God's righteousness’ here means the right standing God gives, and his own saving faithfulness. To ‘establish their own’ means building a standing of one's own instead of receiving his.

‘The end of the law’ uses the Greek word telos. Telos can mean an end, the point where something stops. It can also mean a goal, the thing something aims at, as a race aims at the finish line. Paul may mean either, or both.
passages.ot:
Paul's prayer for his people echoes Israel's own prophets, who prayed for the nation even while warning it. Samuel told Israel, “far be it from me that I should sin against the LORD by ceasing to pray for you” (1 Samuel 12:23).

The law itself pointed to a righteousness that comes from God. Moses promised that “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts” (Deuteronomy 30:6), so that Israel would love him with all its heart. God would do the inner work the people could not do. Paul will quote the same chapter of Deuteronomy in the next verses.

Paul's word ‘zealous’ also had a long history in Israel's Scriptures. Phinehas and Elijah were remembered for zeal for God (Numbers 25:11; 1 Kings 19:10). It was a noble word. Paul does not reject zeal. He says it needs to be joined to knowing what God has done in Christ.
passages.hard:
What does ‘Christ is the end of the law’ mean? Christians read it in more than one way, and these notes do not choose.

Some read ‘end’ as stopping point. Christ ends the law as a way of being right with God. With his coming, the age of the law of Moses as the rule of God's people has closed.

Others read ‘end’ as goal. The law was always pointing to Christ, as an arrow points to its mark. Jesus said, “I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). On this reading, Christ does not throw the law away; he is what it was aiming at.

Many readers hold both: Christ is the goal the law was moving toward, and so, now that he has come, the law's role as the way to righteousness is finished. Paul has already said the law is “holy” (Romans 7:12) and that faith does not nullify it but upholds it (3:31).

What all agree on is the second half of the verse: righteousness is brought ‘to everyone who believes’, Jew and Gentile alike.
passages.asks: Paul prayed for those he disagreed with most. Name someone whose beliefs you think are wrong. Pray for him or her today, as Paul prayed: with desire for their good, not to win.

passages.t: ‘The word is near you’: confess and believe
passages.happening:
Paul sets two kinds of righteousness side by side. Moses writes of the righteousness that is by the law: “The man who does these things will live by them” (verse 5).

“But the righteousness that is by faith says: ‘Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’” (verse 6), that is, to bring Christ down. Or, who will go down into the Abyss, to bring Christ up from the dead (verse 7)? No one needs to. “The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart” (verse 8). It is the word of faith that Paul preaches.

Paul's message is “that if you confess with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved” (verse 9). The heart believes and is justified; the mouth confesses and is saved (verse 10).

Scripture says, “Anyone who believes in Him will never be put to shame” (verse 11). “For there is no difference between Jew and Greek: The same Lord is Lord of all, and gives richly to all who call on Him” (verse 12). “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
‘The Abyss’ means the deep, the realm of the dead. Paul's point is that no one has to climb to heaven or go down to the grave to find Christ. God has already sent him and already raised him. The news has come close.

‘Jesus is Lord’ is one of the oldest Christian confessions. ‘Lord’ is the Greek word kyrios. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament that Jews used, kyrios stood for God's own name. To call Jesus ‘Lord’ was to say something about who he is.

The word was also used of the emperor. In Acts, the Roman governor Festus speaks of the emperor, who was then Nero, as ‘our sovereign one’ (Acts 25:26); the Greek word there means ‘the lord’. So in Rome, the emperor's own city, saying ‘Jesus is Lord’ out loud meant naming where one's highest loyalty lay. It was a public word, and it could cost a person family, work and standing.

This verse is not a formula to be repeated once to be safe forever. ‘Heart’ and ‘mouth’ are two sides of one life: trust inside, and open loyalty outside. Notice what is believed: that God raised Jesus from the dead. The resurrection is at the centre.

‘No difference between Jew and Greek’. Greek here means Gentile. One Lord, the same for all, rich toward everyone.
passages.ot:
Verse 5 quotes Leviticus: “Keep My statutes and My judgments, for the man who does these things will live by them” (Leviticus 18:5). In its setting this is a promise of life in the land to Israel as it keeps God's law.

Verses 6 to 8 echo Deuteronomy 30. There Moses, near the end of his life, tells Israel that God's command is not out of reach: “It is not in heaven, that you should need to ask, ‘Who will ascend into heaven to get it for us and proclaim it, that we may obey it?’” (Deuteronomy 30:12). “But the word is very near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you may obey it” (Deuteronomy 30:14). In Moses' setting, the word is God's law, given and near. Paul reads the passage in the light of Christ: the word now near is the message about Christ. He adds his own short explanations (‘that is, to bring Christ down’), as Jewish teachers often did when they explained a text line by line.

Verse 11 repeats Isaiah 28:16 from 9:33: “the one who believes will never be shaken” (Isaiah 28:16).

Verse 13 quotes Joel: “And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved” (Joel 2:32). In Joel, ‘the LORD’ is Israel's God, and the promise comes with the pouring out of his Spirit “on all people” (Joel 2:28). Peter quoted it at Pentecost (Acts 2:21). Paul, having just called Jesus ‘Lord’, applies it to calling on him.
passages.hard:
Does verse 9 mean that saying a prayer once saves a person, whatever he believes or does afterward? Paul's words are simple, and they are meant to be. Anyone can call, and everyone who calls will be saved. But verse 9 is not a magic sentence. Confessing Jesus as Lord means taking him as one's Lord. Elsewhere Paul writes, “no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except by the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). Churches differ on how a person first comes to faith and how baptism belongs to it; the note on Romans 6:1-4 and the Acts 2 notes set out those differences.

And what of the law? Verse 5 sets the law's way, ‘the man who does these things will live’, against the way of faith. Readers differ on whether Paul sees Leviticus and Deuteronomy as opposed, or whether he reads Deuteronomy as the law itself pointing beyond the law. Many note that Deuteronomy 30 already speaks of God changing the heart (verse 6 of that chapter). These notes do not choose.
passages.asks: ‘The word is near you.’ Ask what you think stands between you and God: a height to climb, a depth to cross. Then read verse 8 again. Ask whether there is a place, a person or a moment where you need to say out loud whom you belong to.

passages.t: ‘How can they hear?’ Israel heard, and God holds out his hands
passages.happening:
Paul asks a chain of questions. “How then can they call on the One in whom they have not believed? And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard? And how can they hear without someone to preach?” (verse 14). And how can anyone preach unless he is sent? As Scripture says, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!” (verse 15).

But not all welcomed the news. Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed our message?” (verse 16). “Consequently, faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ” (verse 17).

Did Israel not hear? They did. “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world” (verse 18). Did Israel not understand? Moses says God will make them jealous by those who are not a nation (verse 19). Isaiah says, “I was found by those who did not seek Me” (verse 20). “But as for Israel he says: ‘All day long I have held out My hands to a disobedient and obstinate people’” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
In Paul's world, news travelled by messengers. A runner carried word of a victory or a new ruler. His arrival was itself good news. Paul's chain of questions runs backward from calling, to believing, to hearing, to preaching, to sending. Each step needs the one before it.

‘Faith comes by hearing.’ The Roman house churches heard Paul's letter read aloud. Most people could not read, so hearing was how nearly everyone met the Scriptures.

Then Paul turns to his question about Israel. They cannot say they did not hear; the message had gone out through the synagogues of the empire for more than twenty years. And yet the last word of the chapter is not a door shut. It is God's hands held out ‘all day long’. The picture is of a parent reaching for a child who turns away, and still reaching.

‘Jealous’ in verse 19 points ahead. In chapter 11 Paul says Gentiles coming to faith will move Israel to jealousy, the good kind that wants what it sees, and so lead them back.
passages.ot:
Paul names five Scriptures in a row.

Verse 15 quotes Isaiah: “How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news” (Isaiah 52:7). There, runners cross the hills to tell Jerusalem that the exile is ending and “Your God reigns” (Isaiah 52:7).

Verse 16 quotes the opening of Isaiah's song of the suffering servant: “Who has believed our message?” (Isaiah 53:1). The message that was not believed is the news of the servant who suffers for others.

Verse 18 quotes a psalm about the heavens: “their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 19:4). In the psalm, the skies speak of God's glory everywhere. Paul borrows the words for the message going out to the world.

Verse 19 quotes the Song of Moses: “So I will make them jealous by those who are not a people” (Deuteronomy 32:21). Israel had provoked God with idols; he would provoke them with outsiders.

Verses 20 and 21 quote Isaiah 65: “I was found by those who did not seek Me” (Isaiah 65:1), and “All day long I have held out My hands to an obstinate people” (Isaiah 65:2). Paul reads the first line of Gentiles and the second of Israel.
passages.hard:
If faith comes by hearing, what about people who never heard of Jesus? Verses 14 and 15 are often read with that question in mind.

Christians answer it in more than one way. Some hold that explicit faith in Christ is needed for salvation, and they find in these verses the urgency of sending messengers. Others hold that salvation is only through Christ, but that God may save some who respond in faith to what they know of him, pointing to passages such as Romans 2:14-16. A smaller number hold that those who never heard will meet Christ at or after death. These notes do not choose. All agree that salvation is God's work through Christ alone and that the Judge of all the earth will do what is just. The site's Honest Answer, ‘What about those who never heard of Jesus?’, sets out the case for each.

Paul's own question in this chapter is a different one. It is not about those who never heard, but about Israel, who did hear (verse 18). And his conclusion is not that God has given up on them. It is that God is still holding out his hands. On any reading, these verses give no ground for contempt toward Jewish people. Paul says Israel's story is not finished, and chapter 11 says so at length.
passages.asks: Someone was sent to you, or you would not have heard. Think of who first told you about Christ, or put a Bible in your hands. Thank God for them. Then ask whom you might be sent to, and what beautiful feet would look like on you this week.
